turns.content: I think phones should be allowed because they help people. Sometimes students need them if something happens at home, and they can also help us look things up. It isn't fair that everyone loses their phones because a few students don't pay attention.

You've taken a clear position — phones should be allowed — and you've given three different reasons. Right now, though, a reader might ask: what's the ONE main thing you most want them to accept? A claim does real work when it says something a thoughtful person could push back on and gives a reason why your side is right. Try writing one sentence that states your position AND gives your strongest reason for it — what would you most want a skeptical reader to walk away believing?

cases.label: Student C
cases.assignment: Some schools have banned personal cell phones during class. Write one paragraph arguing whether your school should allow or ban personal cell phones during class. Take a clear position and support it with reasons and examples.
cases.response: While many worry that cell phones distract students, our school should allow them during class under clear guidelines. Phones are powerful learning tools: students can access research, translate unfamiliar terms, and organize assignments in seconds. A complete ban assumes students cannot learn self-control, yet responsible use is itself a skill worth teaching. Rather than removing phones entirely, teachers could set 'phone-on' and 'phone-off' times, helping students practice the judgment they will need long after high school.

turns.content: While many worry that cell phones distract students, our school should allow them during class under clear guidelines. Phones are powerful learning tools: students can access research, translate unfamiliar terms, and organize assignments in seconds. A complete ban assumes students cannot learn self-control, yet responsible use is itself a skill worth teaching. Rather than removing phones entirely, teachers could set 'phone-on' and 'phone-off' times, helping students practice the judgment they will need long after high school.

You've written a paragraph that takes a clear position and gives the reader three distinct reasons — that's real argumentative work. Here's a question worth sitting with: your third reason (that responsible use is a skill worth teaching) is doing something different from the first two — it's making a claim about *what schools should develop in students*, not just what phones can do. Can you say, in your own words, what that reason is actually asking your reader to believe, and why someone might push back on it?

You've written a paragraph that takes a clear position and covers several angles — that's real work. developmental_profile.control_statement: Produces a genuine, arguable position with a conditional qualifier; claim is present but its alignment with the paragraph's reasons is unconfirmed.
developmental_profile.evidence: First sentence states a conditional position; reasons follow but argue broadly; student has not yet demonstrated awareness of claim-body alignment.

developmental_profile.control_statement: Demonstrates intentional argument structure (claim, reasons, concession, close) in a single paragraph; no concrete examples yet despite assignment requiring them.
developmental_profile.evidence: Paragraph moves through recognizable argument moves with transitional markers; concession/rebuttal present; evidence remains at the level of assertion.

cases.label: Student F
cases.assignment: Some schools have banned personal cell phones during class. Write one paragraph arguing whether your school should allow or ban personal cell phones during class. Take a clear position and support it with reasons and examples.
cases.response: In my opinion the school need to allow the phone in class. Many student use phone for translate the difficult word, this help us to understand the lesson better. Also when we don't understand, we can search fast the information. If the school ban all phone, is more hard for student like me who still learning English. So I think phone can help if we use with respect.

turns.content: In my opinion the school need to allow the phone in class. Many student use phone for translate the difficult word, this help us to understand the lesson better. Also when we don't understand, we can search fast the information. If the school ban all phone, is more hard for student like me who still learning English. So I think phone can help if we use with respect.

You've made a clear argument: phones help students — especially English learners — understand lessons better. That's a real position a reader could agree or disagree with. Right now your opening sentence says 'the school need to allow the phone in class,' which tells us your topic but doesn't yet tell the reader the specific reason that makes your case worth accepting. Can you rewrite that opening sentence so it names not just your position (allow phones) but the key reason that drives your whole argument — the one that makes someone who disagrees stop and think?

telos.audience_or_communicative_purpose: Persuade a reader (likely teacher/classmates) that phones should be allowed in class.
telos.unresolved_ambiguity: Whether 'phones in class' means unrestricted or limited use — student's draft implies responsible/limited use but claim doesn't scope it.

theory.current_telos: Student argues phones should be allowed in class, grounding the claim in ELL learning needs; telos is to clarify and develop a persuasive position with reasons and examples.

communicative_purpose.inferred_from: assignment prompt ('arguing whether') + student's own framing ('I think phone can help')

paragraph_function.purpose: Argue that phones should be allowed in class by offering reasons grounded in learning needs, especially for ELL students.
paragraph_function.contribution_to_whole: This IS the whole piece; the paragraph must carry both the claim and its support.
paragraph_function.coherence: Sentences share a common theme (phones help learning) but shift between general students and personal ELL identity; no single controlling idea stated explicitly.
paragraph_function.development: Two brief reasons offered (translation, information search) plus a personal ELL appeal; minimal elaboration of either reason.
paragraph_function.placement: Single-paragraph argument; opening and closing sentences both restate opinion without adding organizational direction.

evidence_function.function: Illustrate how phones support learning; ground the argument in a relatable scenario.
evidence_function.interpretation_gap: Both examples (translation and searching) are stated but not explained — the reader is not shown WHY these uses constitute a strong reason to allow phones broadly. The ELL appeal is emotionally present but not developed as reasoning.
evidence_function.quality: Relevant to the topic; insufficient to carry a general 'allow phones' claim; no explanation of how examples establish the claim.

coherence_function.intended_relationship: elaboration — each sentence adds a reason or consequence supporting the main position
coherence_function.reader_can_follow: Reader can follow the general direction but the opening sentence doesn't commit to a specific controlling reason, so the paragraph feels like a list of observations rather than a driven argument.

functions_in_play: brief qualification ('if we use with respect')
conclusion_function.completes_purpose: Weakly — it adds a useful qualification but doesn't connect back to the strongest reason or leave the reader with a clear understanding of why the argument should be accepted.
conclusion_function.relationship_to_opening: Mirrors the opening opinion without adding synthesis or significance.
conclusion_function.final_understanding: Reader is left with 'phones can help if used responsibly' — slightly stronger scoping than the opener, but the key reason (ELL/learning support) isn't reinforced.

diagnosed_opportunities: Central claim lacks a governing reason — position stated but not yet a full arguable claim
Evidence is present but uninterpreted — examples dropped without explanation of how they establish the claim
Conclusion restates without synthesizing or reinforcing the strongest reason
ELL identity is a distinctive and potentially powerful warrant but is undeveloped
scaffolding_control.primary_target: Central Claim — the opening sentence needs to embed the key reason so the paragraph has a controlling arguable claim, not just a topic/opinion
scaffolding_control.prioritization_rationale: Claim is the prerequisite: until the opening states an arguable, reasoned position, the evidence and conclusion have nothing to serve. ELL-grounded reasoning is already in the draft — the developmental act is to surface it in the claim.
postponed: evidence interpretation (how examples connect to claim)
scaffolding_control.future_opportunity: Evidence interpretation — helping the student explain WHY translation/searching helps, rather than just stating it

reader_construction.reader_understanding: Reader understands the student wants phones allowed and that phones help with translation and searching. Reader is aware the student is an ELL learner.
likely_reader_questions: Why should phones be allowed for everyone if the main reason is ELL needs?
How does translating help enough to outweigh distraction concerns?
reader_construction.assumed_knowledge: Reader is assumed to accept that translation = better understanding without any elaboration — reasonable inference but underdeveloped.
reader_construction.clarification_needed: What specific kind of phone use is being argued for — any use, or only learning-focused use?
reader_construction.elaboration_needed: How translation/searching actually produces better understanding (the causal step is missing).
reader_construction.precision_risk: 'Allow the phone in class' could mean unrestricted use; the conclusion qualifies this ('with respect') but the claim doesn't.
reader_construction.next_reader_need: A claim that tells the reader not just what the student wants but the reason that makes the position worth accepting.

supporting_frameworks: reader_construction — identifies that the reader needs a reason in the claim
paragraph_function — confirms the paragraph lacks a controlling idea sentence
integration_calibration.calibration_check: Proportionate — the claim is the highest-leverage fix; the student has evidence and a genuine position, so one targeted act (claim revision) is sufficient this turn.
integration_calibration.consistency_check: Yes — a paragraph with a topic-only opener and present-but-uninterpreted evidence would always get claim as the primary target first.
integration_calibration.integration_notes: Reader construction and paragraph function both point to the same gap: the controlling idea sentence. Unified into one target: revise the claim to include the key reason.

instructional_reasoning.element_communicative_purpose: Assert a clear, supportable position the reader is asked to accept — commits the writer to a scoped, reasoned stance.
instructional_reasoning.student_current_organization: Student states an opinion ('I think we should allow phones') and lists reasons but the opening sentence presents a topic/position without embedding a reason; the paragraph's strongest reasoning (ELL learning support) appears mid-paragraph rather than governing the whole.
instructional_reasoning.canonical_performance_structure: State a clear position; embed a reason or scope; make it contestable and supportable.
instructional_reasoning.primary_developmental_tension: Opening sentence is a bare opinion ('school need to allow the phone') rather than a claim that gives the reader a reason to weigh — the ELL/learning-support reasoning that governs the paragraph isn't in the governing sentence.
instructional_reasoning.next_student_act: Revise the opening sentence to embed the key reason alongside the position.
instructional_reasoning.resource_selection_rationale: Brief explanation names the difference between a topic/opinion and a claim-with-reason; focused question directs the student to their own strongest reasoning already in the draft; reminder of assignment grounds the act in the persuasive task.

theory.current_organization: Opinion opener → two reasons (translation, fast information search) → concession to ELL identity → closing restatement. Loosely organized around support claim; no governing thesis sentence that names a reason.
observed_differentiations: distinguishes position from reasons (reasons follow the opener separately)
includes a personal identity element (ELL) as a distinct appeal
observed_integrations: loosely integrates position + reasons + personal experience into one paragraph
observed_coordinations: 'Also' and 'So' coordinate additive and causal relationships across sentences
theory.emerging_intentional_control: Student is beginning to organize argument around reasons; intentional use of personal experience as warrant is emerging.
unresolved_tensions: Claim scope: 'allow phones' vs 'allow phones for learning purposes'
Evidence interpretation absent — reasons stated but not explained
possible_reorganizations: Revise opener to embed key reason → paragraph gains a controlling claim
Add one sentence after translation example explaining HOW it helps → evidence gains interpretation
current_uncertainty: Whether student understands distinction between stating a position and making an arguable claim
Whether ELL framing is the student's intended primary reason or incidental detail
supporting_evidence: Student already has the strongest reason (ELL learning support) in the draft
Closing qualification ('with respect') shows some awareness of scope
complicating_evidence: Two reasons given (translation, searching) — unclear which is primary
Language errors present but do not obscure meaning
alternative_interpretations: Student may already understand claim-with-reason intuitively but lacks the sentence-level control to write it
ELL framing may be the student's most authentic and central reason, not a secondary appeal

The strongest reason is already in your paragraph (phones help students understand, especially English learners). Can you rewrite that first sentence so it says both your position AND that key reason?

intervention.interpretation: Student has a genuine position and real reasons; the opening sentence is an opinion statement rather than an arguable claim with a reason embedded.
intervention.instruction: A persuasive claim does two things: it states your position AND gives the reader a reason to weigh. 'Allow phones' is your position; the reason (phones help students understand, especially ELL students) is what makes it arguable rather than just a preference. Writers put that reason in the claim so the reader knows from the first sentence what the whole argument is earning.
intervention.timing_rationale: Student lacks the claim-with-reason form — the concept needs naming before the invitation to revise; instruction reorganizes present organization rather than replacing it.
intervention.writing_not_content_check: Teaches the communicative function of embedding a reason in a claim (writing principle); does not supply the reason or the sentence — student draws on their own draft content.

developmental_profile.control_statement: States a clear position on the assigned topic but does not yet embed a governing reason in the claim sentence; reasons appear separately in the body.
developmental_profile.evidence: Opening sentence 'school need to allow the phone' is a topic/opinion; strongest reason (ELL learning support) appears mid-paragraph rather than governing the whole.

developmental_profile.control_statement: Produces relevant examples (translation, searching) but does not yet interpret them — states what the examples are without explaining how they establish the claim.
